tagline: A short, urgent letter from Jude, brother of James, calling believers to contend for the faith against teachers who turn grace into license, and ending in one of Scripture's great doxologies.
overview:
Jude meant to write a warm letter about the salvation he shared with his readers. Instead he wrote an alarm. Certain people had slipped into the church unnoticed, and they were turning the grace of God into permission for immorality and denying Jesus Christ as Master and Lord. Jude urges his readers to contend earnestly for the faith that was handed down once for all to God's people.

Most of the letter is a dense string of examples drawn from Israel's Scriptures and Jewish tradition: Israel in the wilderness, the angels who left their proper place, Sodom and Gomorrah, Cain, Balaam, and Korah. Jude piles up images from nature to describe the intruders: hidden reefs, waterless clouds, fruitless trees, wild waves, wandering stars. He also cites two traditions that don't appear in the Old Testament: a dispute between the archangel Michael and the devil over the body of Moses, and a prophecy of Enoch that matches a passage in the book called 1 Enoch.

The letter ends not with fear but with care and praise. Jude tells the faithful to build themselves up, pray in the Spirit, keep themselves in God's love, and show mercy to those who doubt. His closing blessing, to him who is able to keep you from stumbling, has been sung and prayed in churches for two thousand years.
author:
The writer calls himself Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James (verse 1). The name is the Greek form of Judah, and in English Bibles it is usually rendered Judas elsewhere. Since the James mentioned without further explanation is almost certainly James the brother of Jesus, the well-known leader of the Jerusalem church (Galatians 1:19), the traditional view is that this Jude is also a brother of Jesus. Mark 6:3 lists a Judas among Jesus' brothers. Notably, Jude doesn't call himself the Lord's brother but his servant, which many readers take as a mark of humility.

The second-century writer Hegesippus, as quoted by Eusebius, tells of grandsons of Jude, farmers in Palestine, who were brought before the emperor Domitian and released. Some modern scholars think the letter is pseudonymous, written later in Jude's name, pointing to its polished Greek and to verse 17, which looks back on the apostles as if from a distance. Others respond that a Galilean family could have had good Greek, that a secretary may have helped, and that a later forger would more likely have claimed to be the brother of Jesus outright.
date: Dating depends on authorship. Those who accept that Jude the brother of Jesus wrote it usually date it between about AD 50 and 80. Those who see it as pseudonymous date it later in the first century or early in the second. There is a close relationship with 2 Peter 2, which contains much of the same material in the same order. Most scholars think 2 Peter drew on Jude, which would place Jude earlier; a minority argues the reverse.
setting:
The letter doesn't say where its readers lived. Its heavy use of Jewish Scripture and tradition suggests a community of Jewish believers, or a mixed church steeped in Jewish ways of reading, perhaps in Palestine, Syria, or elsewhere in the eastern Mediterranean. The problem is internal. The intruders take part in the church's love feasts, the shared meals at which early Christians ate together and often celebrated the Lord's Supper. They claim spiritual authority, perhaps through visions (Jude calls them dreamers), reject authority, and use freedom as cover for sexual immorality and greed.

Jude draws on writings that were widely read among Jews of his day. The prophecy in verses 14-15 closely matches 1 Enoch 1:9, part of a collection of writings attributed to the Enoch of Genesis 5 and composed over the last centuries before Christ. Fragments of 1 Enoch in Aramaic were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, and the book is part of the Bible of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church to this day. The story of Michael disputing with the devil over Moses' body (verse 9) is not in the Old Testament; early Christian writers, including Origen, said it came from a work known as the Assumption of Moses. A text called the Testament of Moses survives, but its ending is lost, so the exact source of Jude's story cannot now be checked.
purpose: Jude writes to rouse the church to defend the faith it had received and to recognize the intruders for what they were. His long list of examples is meant to show that God has always judged those who reject his authority and turn his gifts into occasions for sin. But the letter's aim is pastoral, not merely polemical: Jude wants the faithful to stay in God's love, strengthen one another, and reach out with mercy to those wavering or caught in error.
story: Jude sits near the end of the New Testament, among the general letters, written as the first generation of believers was giving way to the next. It looks back across the whole of Israel's story, from Cain and Enoch to the exodus, the wilderness, and Balaam, to warn a church that the same patterns of rebellion can reappear inside God's people. It also looks forward to the Lord's coming with his holy ones to judge, and to the mercy of Jesus Christ that brings eternal life. The next book, Revelation, takes up that forward look on a grand scale.
christ: Jude calls himself a servant of Jesus Christ and names him our only Master and Lord (verse 4). Believers are kept in Jesus Christ (verse 1) and await his mercy that leads to eternal life (verse 21). In verse 5, several early and important manuscripts say that it was Jesus who delivered Israel out of Egypt, and the BSB follows them; others read the Lord. If Jesus is the original reading, Jude identifies Christ with the God who acted in Israel's history. The closing doxology gives glory to the only God our Savior through Jesus Christ our Lord, from before all time and forever.
reading:
Jude is compact and allusive. Read it with the Old Testament stories it cites in mind: Numbers 14 on the wilderness generation, Genesis 6 and 19, Genesis 4 on Cain, Numbers 22-24 and 31 on Balaam, and Numbers 16 on Korah. Watch for Jude's fondness for threes, which organizes much of the letter.

Readers are often troubled by Jude's use of 1 Enoch. Quoting a book is not the same as endorsing everything in it; Paul quotes Greek poets (Acts 17:28; Titus 1:12) without making them Scripture. Jude treats this particular saying as a true prophecy, and Christians have differed on what that implies about the book as a whole. Another common misreading takes the harsh images as license for harshness toward anyone one disagrees with. Jude's final instructions are to show mercy, snatch people from the fire, and keep oneself from contamination, not to write anyone off.

structure.title: Greeting
structure.summary: Jude, servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, greets those who are called, loved, and kept.

structure.title: Contend for the faith
structure.summary: Jude changes his plan and urges his readers to fight for the faith once delivered, because ungodly people have slipped in, twisting grace and denying Christ.

structure.title: Examples of judgment and portraits of the intruders
structure.summary: Examples from Israel's history and tradition show God's judgment on rebellion, and vivid images describe the intruders, ending with Enoch's prophecy of the Lord's coming.

structure.title: Remember, build, keep, and show mercy
structure.summary: The readers should remember the apostles' warning, build themselves up in faith and prayer, keep themselves in God's love, and show mercy to those who doubt or are in danger.

structure.title: Doxology
structure.summary: Glory to the God who is able to keep believers from stumbling and present them blameless and joyful before him.

themes.title: The faith once delivered
themes.body: Jude speaks of the faith as something entrusted once for all to the saints (verse 3), a body of teaching received, not invented. The church does not revise it to suit its appetites; it guards it and passes it on.

themes.title: Grace is not license
themes.body: The intruders turned the grace of God into a license for immorality. Jude insists that the same God who saves also judges, and that grace frees people from sin rather than for it.

themes.title: Judgment in history
themes.body: Jude's examples, from the wilderness generation to Sodom and Gomorrah, teach that God's patience is not indifference. Past judgments serve as warnings to those inside the covenant community, not only outside it.

themes.title: Kept by God
themes.body: The letter begins with those who are kept in Jesus Christ and ends with the God who is able to keep them from stumbling. Between those bookends, believers are told to keep themselves in God's love. Divine keeping and human effort stand side by side.

themes.title: Mercy toward the wavering
themes.body: After fierce warnings, Jude's last instructions are about mercy: to those who doubt, to those who must be pulled from the fire, and to those who must be helped with caution. Contending for the faith never cancels compassion for people.

keyChapters.why: The whole letter: the call to contend for the faith, the examples of judgment, the use of Enoch and the Moses tradition, and the great closing doxology.

parts.body:
Jude is a short letter, twenty-five verses, and it reads aloud in about five minutes. Its writer meant to send something warm. “Beloved, although I made every effort to write to you about the salvation we share, I felt it necessary to write and urge you to contend earnestly for the faith entrusted once for all to the saints” (verse 3). He wrote an alarm instead.

The reason: “For certain men have crept in among you unnoticed” (verse 4). They had slipped into the church. They were turning ‘the grace of our God into a license for immorality’, and denying ‘our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ’.

Most of the letter is a dense string of examples, drawn from Israel's Scriptures and from Jewish writings of the time: Israel in the wilderness, the angels who left their place, Sodom and Gomorrah, Cain, Balaam and Korah. Jude piles up pictures from nature to describe the intruders: hidden reefs, clouds without water, fruitless trees, wild waves, wandering stars. He also uses two stories that are not in the Old Testament: the archangel Michael disputing with the devil over the body of Moses, and a prophecy of Enoch that matches a passage in the book called 1 Enoch.

But the letter does not end in fear. It ends in care and praise. The faithful are to build themselves up, pray in the Spirit, keep themselves in God's love, and show mercy to those who doubt. And its last lines, “Now to Him who is able to keep you from stumbling” (verse 24), have been prayed and sung in churches ever since.

The writer calls himself “Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James” (verse 1). Jude is the Greek form of the name Judah; English Bibles usually call other men of that name Judas. The James he names without explaining is almost certainly James the brother of Jesus, the well-known leader of the church in Jerusalem (Galatians 1:19). So the traditional view is that Jude, too, was a brother of Jesus. Mark lists a Judas among Jesus' brothers (Mark 6:3). Like James, he did not believe in Jesus during his ministry (John 7:5), but came to faith afterward.

Notice that he does not call himself ‘the Lord's brother’. He calls himself a servant. Many readers see humility in that.

The historian Eusebius, quoting the second-century writer Hegesippus, tells of grandsons of Jude, working farmers in Palestine, who were brought before the emperor Domitian because they were descended from David, and were released.

Some modern scholars think the letter was written later in Jude's name. They point to its polished Greek, and to verse 17, which looks back on the apostles as if from a distance. Others answer that a family from Galilee could have had good Greek, that a secretary may have helped, and that a later writer using his name would more likely have called himself the brother of Jesus outright. These notes do not choose.

The early church received Jude slowly. Jerome, late in the 300s, noted that many rejected it because it quotes 1 Enoch. Eusebius counted it among the books that were disputed but widely known, and the Syriac churches long read a New Testament without it. The Muratorian list, usually dated to the late second century, already includes it. In the end the whole church received it as Scripture.

The date depends on who wrote it. Those who hold that Jude the brother of Jesus wrote it usually date it between about AD 50 and 80. Those who think it was written in his name date it later in the first century or early in the second.

The letter does not say where its readers lived. Its heavy use of Jewish Scripture and tradition suggests a church of Jewish believers, or a mixed church used to Jewish ways of reading, perhaps in Palestine, Syria or elsewhere in the eastern Mediterranean.

The danger was inside. The intruders took part in the church's ‘love feasts’ (verse 12), the shared meals at which early Christians ate together, the rich supplying the poor, often with the Lord's Supper. They claimed spiritual authority, perhaps through visions; Jude calls them ‘dreamers’ (verse 8). They rejected authority, and they used freedom as cover for sexual immorality and greed.

Jude is carefully made, and it loves threes. Its readers are called, loved and kept (verse 1). He wishes them mercy, peace and love (verse 2).

Greeting (verses 1-2).

Contend for the faith (verses 3-4). Jude changes his plan, because ungodly people have crept in.

Examples and portraits (verses 5-16). Three examples of judgment: Israel in the wilderness, the angels, Sodom and Gomorrah. Then the intruders described, with three more figures, Cain, Balaam and Korah, and a string of pictures from nature, ending with Enoch's prophecy. Again and again Jude says ‘these men’ (verses 8, 10, 12, 16, 19), applying each example to the intruders.

Remember, build, keep, and show mercy (verses 17-23). The apostles' warning, and what the faithful are to do.

Praise (verses 24-25). Glory to the God who is able to keep them.

The letter is framed by keeping: those ‘kept in Jesus Christ’ (verse 1), ‘keep yourselves in the love of God’ (verse 21), and the God who is able ‘to keep you from stumbling’ (verse 24).

Jude's call is to ‘contend earnestly for the faith entrusted once for all to the saints’ (verse 3). The word for contend comes from the world of athletic contests, a hard struggle. It appears only here in the New Testament. Jude is not calling for violence. He is calling for the determination of an athlete.

‘The faith entrusted once for all’ is a body of teaching received, not invented. The church does not rewrite it to suit its appetites. It guards it and passes it on.

The intruders were doing two things. They turned grace into licence: since God forgives, they said in effect, you may live as you like. And they denied ‘our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ’. The word for Master, despotēs, is one often used of God.

Two cautions belong here. First, Jude's fierce words are about people who were turning grace into a cover for immorality and denying Christ, not about every person a believer disagrees with. Second, the same letter ends with mercy. Contending for the faith never cancels compassion for people.

Jude reminds his readers of what they already know (verse 5). God rescued his people from Egypt, and afterward destroyed those who did not believe. Here the old copies differ. Several early and important manuscripts say that it was ‘Jesus’ who delivered his people out of Egypt, and the BSB follows them; others read ‘the Lord’ or ‘God’. If ‘Jesus’ is the original, Jude names Christ as the God who acted in Israel's history.

Then the angels: “the angels who did not stay within their own domain but abandoned their proper dwelling—these He has kept in eternal chains under darkness, bound for judgment on that great day” (verse 6). Many readers think Jude means the ‘sons of God’ of Genesis 6:1-4, read as heavenly beings, as the book of 1 Enoch read them: watchers who took human wives and were imprisoned in darkness until judgment. Others read Genesis 6 differently, as the family of Seth or as powerful kings, as the notes on Genesis 6 set out, and so take Jude more generally, of angels who rebelled. These notes do not choose. 2 Peter 2:4 says the same thing in other words.

Then Sodom and Gomorrah, which ‘indulged in sexual immorality and pursued strange flesh’ (verse 7). Christians read this verse in more than one way, as they read Genesis 19. All agree that the men of Sodom tried to rape two strangers, and that this was monstrous. The traditional reading, held by most churches through history, sees the same-sex nature of the demand as part of what Jude condemns, along with the violence. Another reading holds that the point is violent cruelty to strangers, and notes that Jude's ‘strange flesh’ (in Greek, ‘other flesh’) has been read by some as the angels, since the visitors to Sodom were angels. These notes take no side on that question here. On both readings nothing in this verse gives anyone a reason for contempt toward any person.

If you are gay, or love someone who is, you are met with respect here. If these verses weigh on you, talk with a trusted pastor or friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

The point of the three examples is the same. God's patience is not indifference. Those inside God's people are not exempt from his judgment.

parts.h: Michael, Moses and Enoch: books outside the Old Testament
parts.body:
Jude uses two traditions that are not in the Old Testament.

In verse 9 he says that ‘even the archangel Michael, when he disputed with the devil over the body of Moses, did not presume to bring a slanderous charge against him, but said, “The Lord rebuke you!”’ Deuteronomy says only that God buried Moses and that ‘no one to this day knows the location of his grave’ (Deuteronomy 34:6). The story of Michael's dispute is not there. Early Christian writers, including Origen, said it came from a work known as the Assumption of Moses. A related text, the Testament of Moses, survives, but its ending is lost, so the passage Jude drew on cannot now be checked.

In verses 14 and 15 he quotes a prophecy: “Enoch, the seventh from Adam, also prophesied about them: ‘Behold, the Lord is coming with myriads of His holy ones to execute judgment on everyone’” (verses 14-15). These words closely match a passage in 1 Enoch (1:9). 1 Enoch is a collection of Jewish writings named after the Enoch of Genesis 5, who ‘walked with God’, written over the last centuries before Christ. Fragments of it in Aramaic were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls. It was widely read by Jews in Jude's day, and it is part of the Bible of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church to this day.

Does quoting it make 1 Enoch Scripture? This troubled some in the early church. Jerome noted that many rejected Jude for that reason, while Tertullian argued that Jude's use of Enoch showed the book had value. Christians have generally answered in one of several ways. Many say that quoting a book is not the same as calling it Scripture. Paul quotes Greek poets (Acts 17:28; Titus 1:12) and a Jewish tradition about Jannes and Jambres (2 Timothy 3:8) without treating those sources as Scripture. On this view, Jude affirms that this one saying is a true prophecy of the Lord's coming, which agrees with the Old Testament, without making the rest of 1 Enoch Scripture. Others note that Jude was writing to readers who valued these works, and used them as common ground. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church, by contrast, includes 1 Enoch in its Bible. For most churches, Jude's use of these traditions shows how deeply the first Christians lived in the Jewish world of their day.

Notice, too, what Jude does with Michael's story. Even the archangel did not hurl insults at the devil; he left the rebuke to the Lord. Michael's words echo the prophet: “The LORD rebukes you, Satan” (Zechariah 3:2). The intruders, by contrast, ‘slander what they do not understand’ (verse 10).

Much of Jude 4 to 18 is very close to 2 Peter 2:1 to 3:3: the same images, in much the same order. False teachers who have slipped in; the angels who sinned; Sodom and Gomorrah; Balaam; waterless clouds and springs; scoffers in the last days.

Most scholars think 2 Peter used Jude, because Jude's version is shorter and sharper, and because 2 Peter leaves out Jude's direct use of 1 Enoch and of the dispute over Moses' body. Others think Jude used 2 Peter, or that both drew on a common source. These notes do not choose. Borrowing between writers would not have troubled ancient readers.

The oldest surviving copy of Jude is a papyrus known as P72, from about the 200s or 300s, which holds 1 Peter, 2 Peter and Jude together.

After the fierce middle, Jude turns to his ‘beloved’ (verses 17, 20). First, remember. The apostles had warned that ‘In the last times there will be scoffers’ (verse 18). The trouble is not a sign that the faith has failed. It was foretold.

Then four things to do, one of them three times over. “But you, beloved, by building yourselves up in your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God as you await the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ to bring you eternal life” (verses 20-21). Build up. Pray. Keep. Wait. God keeps them (verse 1, verse 24), and they are to keep themselves in his love. The two stand side by side.

And then mercy. “And indeed, have mercy on those who doubt; save others by snatching them from the fire; and to still others show mercy tempered with fear” (verses 22-23). Jude's last instructions are not about the intruders. They are about the wavering. Those who doubt are to receive mercy, not suspicion. Some need to be pulled from danger. Others need mercy with care, so that the helper is not drawn into the same sin.

The faithful are to reach out, not to write people off.

parts.h: Jesus in Jude, and the closing praise
parts.body:
Jude calls Jesus ‘our only Master and Lord’ (verse 4), using a word for Master often applied to God. If ‘Jesus’ is the original reading in verse 5, Jude names Christ as the one who delivered Israel out of Egypt. Believers are ‘kept in Jesus Christ’ (verse 1), and they wait for ‘the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ’ that leads to eternal life (verse 21). The Lord who comes ‘with myriads of His holy ones’ (verse 14) was, for the early Christians, Christ himself.

The letter ends with one of the great prayers of praise in the New Testament. “Now to Him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you unblemished in His glorious presence, with great joy— to the only God our Savior be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority through Jesus Christ our Lord before all time, and now, and for all eternity. Amen” (verses 24-25).

After warnings about people who fall, the last word is about the God who keeps. The faithful are not held up by their own grip. They are kept by one who is able, and they will stand before him ‘with great joy’.

Jude assumes his readers know the Old Testament well (verse 5), and he moves through it quickly.

The wilderness: God brought Israel out of Egypt, and those who would not believe died in the desert. “Your bodies will fall in this wilderness” (Numbers 14:29).

Sodom and Gomorrah: “Then the LORD rained down sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah” (Genesis 19:24).

Cain, Balaam and Korah (verse 11) had become stock examples of envy, greed and rebellion. Cain killed his brother (Genesis 4). Balaam took fees to curse Israel: “The elders of Moab and Midian departed with the fees for divination in hand” (Numbers 22:7). Korah led a rebellion against Moses and Aaron (Numbers 16).

Enoch ‘the seventh from Adam’ is the Enoch of Genesis 5: “Enoch walked with God, and then he was no more, because God had taken him away” (Genesis 5:24). The coming of the Lord with his holy ones echoes Moses' blessing, where the LORD “came with myriads of holy ones” (Deuteronomy 33:2), and Zechariah: “Then the LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with Him” (Zechariah 14:5).

The picture of people snatched from the fire comes from the prophets: “Is not this man a firebrand snatched from the fire?” (Zechariah 3:2).

It is not a licence for harshness toward anyone you disagree with. Its fierce words are about people who turned grace into licence and denied Christ, and its last instructions are mercy.

It is not a claim that 1 Enoch or the Assumption of Moses is Scripture. Quoting a book is not the same as calling it Scripture.

It is not a reason for contempt toward any person. Whatever reading of verse 7 a reader holds, these notes find nothing in it that permits contempt.

And it is not a letter of fear. It begins and ends with God's keeping.

Read it aloud in one sitting; it takes about five minutes. Then read it again with the Old Testament stories it uses: Numbers 14 on the wilderness, Genesis 6 and 19, Genesis 4 on Cain, Numbers 22 to 24 and 31 on Balaam, and Numbers 16 on Korah.

Count the threes. Notice how often Jude says ‘these men’, and how often he says ‘keep’.

Read 2 Peter 2 beside it, and notice what each includes and leaves out.

Where readers differ, on who wrote it, on the angels, on verse 7, on how to treat 1 Enoch, read more than one view before you settle, and hold your own view as one who may yet be taught.

And end where Jude ends. Pray his last two verses.

The notes on the chapter go through it passage by passage in plain words.

words.line: Greek epagōnizomai, to struggle hard, as in an athletic contest. Only here in the New Testament (1:3).
The teaching ‘entrusted once for all to the saints’, received and handed on (1:3).
Greek despotēs, a word often used of God; here of Jesus Christ (1:4).
Greek tēreō, to keep, guard or hold. It frames the letter (1:1, 6, 13, 21).
Those who left their proper dwelling, held for judgment (1:6).
A chief angel. Michael, who also appears in Daniel (1:9).
The church's shared meals, often with the Lord's Supper (1:12).
Greek spilas, a rock under the water that wrecks ships; some read ‘stains’ (1:12).
Stars off course, useless to sailors who steered by them (1:13).
Mockers who follow their own desires, as the apostles foretold (1:18).
Shown to those who doubt, and to others with care (1:2, 21-23).
A prayer of praise giving glory to God, like verses 24-25.

map.title: The one place on this map

places.name: Sodom and Gomorrah
places.line: The cities Jude gives as ‘an example’ of judgment (1:7; Genesis 19). Where they stood is not known. Drawn at the south end of the Dead Sea, one of the places proposed, roughly.

teaching.mapNote: Jude names two places on earth: Egypt (verse 5) and Sodom and Gomorrah (verse 7). The map shows Sodom and Gomorrah alone, drawn roughly at the south end of the Dead Sea, one of the places proposed; where they stood is not known. Egypt lies beyond the edge of this map. The letter does not say where it was written or where its readers lived.
